title: Rib Joint Play
purpose: Joint play assessment (and mobilisation) of the costotransverse joints of ribs 2-12 to judge joint reactivity, end-feel and capsular restriction.
structure: Costotransverse (costotransversal) joints; rib angle (angulus costae) and the transverse processes of the thoracic spine.
procedure: Patient prone with the head turned toward the examined side and that arm hanging off the bench so the scapula protracts; the examiner stands on the opposite side. Ribs 2-7: the hypothenar of the fixating hand lies on the contralateral transverse process of the segment and the one above; with a cross grip the hypothenar of the working hand lies on the rib angle so the forearm points ventral, lateral and caudal; joint play and end-feel are assessed while the patient exhales. Ribs 8-12: same position, but the hands are switched so the working forearm points ventral, lateral and cranial. Limited joint play can be treated with the same technique as a mobilisation dosed with Maitland grades.
positive: Not a positive/negative test: limited joint play or an abnormal end-feel of the costotransverse joint compared with neighbouring segments or the other side.

accuracy.source: Reliability only: Heiderscheit & Boissonnault 2008 and Beynon et al. 2018 found only slight agreement for thoracic and costovertebral mobility/stiffness assessment

notes: Assessment-and-treatment page rather than a diagnostic test; the source rates its clinical value as weak because inter-rater agreement is only slight. ⚠ The text spells the first author 'Heiderscheidt' while the reference list reads Heiderscheit. Related pages: first rib assessment, cervical rotation lateral flexion test.

title: First Rib Assessment
purpose: Direct mobility assessment of the first rib for hypomobility when evaluating thoracic outlet symptoms or pain at the cervicothoracic junction.
structure: First rib and its joints with T1; upper thoracic aperture; upper trapezius slackened by lateral flexion.
procedure: Three versions. Sitting: the examiner stands behind, locates T1, rotates the head toward the test side (brings the first rib posteriorly) and adds lateral flexion to slacken the trapezius, fixing the position with the elbow on the sternum; the MCP 1 is placed on the first rib and pushes caudal, ventral and medial (toward the contralateral ASIS) while end-feel and symptom reproduction are judged and compared with the other side. Supine: the patient lies slightly diagonal, head rotated toward the test side, one hand braces the cervical spine with slight occipital traction; the MCP 1 lies flat on the rib, the hand is locked against the examiner's pelvis and the body drives a ventral, caudal and medial force; a cross grip is an alternative. Prone: identical to the supine version in prone.
positive: Not a positive/negative test: reduced first rib movement, a hard end-feel or reproduction of symptoms compared with the other side.

accuracy.source: Reliability only: Fjellner et al. 1999 weighted kappa 0.06 for first rib range-of-motion assessment

notes: Three videos (sitting, supine, prone). Inter-examiner reliability is very low (weighted kappa 0.06), so a finding should not stand alone. The cervical rotation lateral flexion test is the indirect alternative; rib joint play covers ribs 2-12.

title: Cervical Rotation Lateral Flexion Test
purpose: Screens for first rib hypomobility (elevated first rib) in patients with thoracic outlet symptoms or limited cervical range of motion.
structure: First rib and its costotransverse joint in the upper thoracic aperture; brachial plexus irritation is the proposed mechanism (Lindgren).
procedure: The patient sits. The head is rotated away from the affected side, then lateral flexion is added in the opposite direction so that the ear moves toward the chest.
positive: No lateral flexion movement along the axis of the costotransverse joint, or a bony restriction blocks the movement.

accuracy.source: Lindgren et al. 1992: inter-rater kappa 1.0 in 23 patients; a positive test correlated with limited first rib elevation on cineradiography

notes: Only one small study (n = 23) has ever described the test, so the clinical value is questionable despite the perfect kappa. ⚠ The text spells the author 'Lindren'; the reference list reads Lindgren (1990 description, 1992 reliability/validity). Direct first rib assessment is the alternative.

title: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome Explained
purpose: Explanation page: definition and classification of thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS), the compression intervals and the list of provocation tests.
structure: Brachial plexus and subclavian vessels in the interscalene triangle, the costoclavicular space and the retropectoralis minor space.
procedure: Not a test. TOS is a symptom complex rather than an ICD diagnosis; it is made by excluding other causes of neurological or vascular arm symptoms such as cervical radicular syndrome and carpal tunnel syndrome. The page divides TOS into four classifications and lists the intervals where neural or vascular entrapment occurs. Davidovic et al. 2003: incidence up to 8%, rare in children, male-to-female ratio 1:2 to 1:4; 98% of causes neurogenic, 2% vascular compression.
positive: n/a. Common tests listed: Adson test, Eden/military brace test, Wright's test, Tinel's sign, Morley/brachial plexus compression test, Cyriax release test, costoclavicular manoeuvre/Halstead test.
notes: ⚠ The four-type classification table and the list of entrapment intervals are images on the source page and are not in its text; this record only states that they exist. References: Davidovic 2003, Watson et al. 2009 (part 1) and 2010 (part 2).

title: Neurological Thoracic Outlet Syndrome
purpose: Criteria page: the Society for Vascular Surgery reporting standards (Illig et al. 2016) that define neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome (nTOS).
structure: Brachial plexus at the scalene triangle and at the pectoralis minor insertion.
procedure: Not a test. nTOS is defined by 3 of the following 4: (1) local findings: history of symptoms consistent with irritation or inflammation at the compression site (scalene triangle or pectoralis insertion) with referred pain to the chest wall, axilla, upper back, shoulder, trapezius region, neck or head (including headache), and pain on palpation of that area; (2) peripheral findings: arm or hand symptoms of nerve compression (numbness, pain, paraesthesia, vasomotor changes, weakness, wasting in extreme cases), often worsened by manoeuvres that narrow the outlet (arms overhead) or stretch the plexus (dangling, driving, walking/running), and reproduced by palpation or by provocative manoeuvres such as the Roos test (elevated arm stress test) or ULTT1; (3) absence of other reasonably likely diagnoses (cervical disc disease, shoulder disease, carpal tunnel syndrome, complex regional pain syndrome, brachial neuritis); (4) a positive response to a properly performed test injection in those who undergo it.
positive: n/a (criteria page). Most patients have symptoms for more than 6 months, deteriorate over time and have a trauma history, but these are not required.
notes: The source stresses that the subjective nature of many of these findings keeps the validity of the nTOS diagnosis controversial. Lists the same common TOS tests as the TOS explained page.

title: Morley Test
purpose: Provocation test for thoracic outlet syndrome that compresses the neurovascular bundle in the supraclavicular fossa (brachial plexus compression test).
structure: Brachial plexus and subclavian vessels in the supraclavicular fossa (interscalene triangle).
procedure: The patient sits upright with the arms at the sides. The examiner compresses the supraclavicular fossa for 30 seconds.
positive: Reproduction of an aching sensation and the typical localised paraesthesia, not mere tenderness of the area.

accuracy.source: No diagnostic accuracy study exists (Watson et al. 2009)

notes: Clinical value questionable because no sensitivity or specificity has been reported. Fullness or a palpable hard mass in the supraclavicular fossa may indicate a true structural lesion causing vascular or true neurological TOS and must itself be examined. The test is probably positive in both cervical radiculopathy and TOS, so it is unlikely to distinguish them.

title: Wright’s Test
purpose: Provocation test for thoracic outlet syndrome: the first part narrows the retropectoralis minor space, the second part implicates the costoclavicular interval.
structure: Retropectoralis minor space and costoclavicular space; brachial plexus and subclavian artery (radial pulse).
procedure: The patient sits comfortably. Part 1: the arm is passively brought into 90° abduction and external rotation without tilting the head, the elbow flexed no more than 45°, and held for 1 minute while the examiner monitors symptom onset and the quality of the radial pulse. Part 2: the test is repeated in hyperabduction (end-range abduction). Other authors add cervical flexion, extension and rotation to each side.
positive: A decrease of the radial pulse and/or reproduction of the patient's symptoms.

accuracy.source: Gillard et al. 2001: the unclear description of how the test was performed prevents any accuracy statement

notes: Clinical value in practice is questionable.

title: Roos Test
purpose: Elevated arm stress test for thoracic outlet syndrome, believed to stress all three intervals because the position tensions the arterial, venous and neural structures.
structure: Interscalene triangle, costoclavicular space and retropectoralis minor space.
procedure: The patient sits with the head neutral, arms abducted and externally rotated to 90° and elbows flexed to 90°, then opens and closes the fingers for up to 3 minutes. The examiner watches for dropping of the arm (fatigue or arterial compromise), compares the colour of the distal extremity left versus right and monitors symptom onset.
positive: The patient cannot maintain the elevation for 3 minutes, or symptoms are induced.

accuracy.source: Gillard et al. 2001, Joint Bone Spine (48 patients; no MRI gold standard)

notes: Low specificity and no MRI reference standard: the source rates the clinical value as rather weak.

title: Referred Pain Thoracic Spine
purpose: Screening page: recognising true visceral pain and visceral referred pain that masquerades as thoracic or mid/upper back pain, with interview questions per organ system.
structure: Viscera sharing segmental innervation with the thoracic spine (cardiovascular, pulmonary and digestive organs); somatic structures with the same segmental innervation receive the referred pain.
procedure: Not a test. True visceral pain is poorly defined and felt in the midline (lower sternum or upper abdomen) because visceral sensory innervation is sparse and diverges widely in the CNS; it can refer to densely innervated somatic structures with the same segmental innervation. History items by system: cardiovascular (heart trouble, chest pain or pressure, palpitations, smoking, hypertension, shortness of breath including nocturnal, limb swelling, family history, elevated cholesterol); pulmonary (smoking, dyspnoea, wheezing, prolonged cough, sputum amount/colour, asthma, emphysema, pneumonia, tuberculosis); digestive (dysphagia, nausea/heartburn, vomiting, food intolerances, constipation, diarrhoea, stool colour change, rectal bleeding, jaundice, liver or gallbladder history; the large intestine, sigmoid colon and oesophagus do not refer to the thoracic spine); locomotor tract (insidious symptoms in multiple joints suggest inflammatory disease). Start with general questions, dig deeper if positive, and explain why you ask.
positive: A pattern suggesting serious pathology: symptoms that do not vary with position or movement and are present at rest, especially pain waking the patient at night; diffuse, dull, vague pain that may build rhythmically, or cramping from hollow-viscus spasm; symptoms tied to eating, bowel or bladder fullness, urination or defecation; insidious onset without trauma; fever, chills, nausea, unexplained weight loss, malaise, vomiting, changes in bowel habits, rectal or vaginal bleeding for more than 1-2 weeks; age, sex, occupation and ethnicity as risk factors. No single question decides; the aim is to refer out, not to diagnose the organ.
notes: ⚠ The list of organs that refer pain to the thoracic spine is an image on the source page and is not in its text. ⚠ The text says ulnar-side arm symptoms mimicking C8 radiculopathy or ulnar nerve entrapment may be a 'pancast' tumour (Pancoast tumour). ⚠ The Sikandar 2012 sentence reads 'somatic pain can be distinguished from visceral pain as it is often associated with marked autonomic phenomena'; in that reference the autonomic phenomena (pallor, sweating, nausea, GI disturbance, changes in temperature, blood pressure and heart rate) and strong affective responses belong to visceral pain. The reference list is printed twice. Companion pages: referred pain cervical spine, referred pain lumbar spine.

title: Thoracic Spine Mobility
purpose: Treatment: five drills to mobilise the thoracic spine (reduced mobility with prolonged sitting, increased kyphosis, forward head posture, limited overhead reach).
structure: Thoracic spine and kyphosis; cervicothoracic junction; overhead shoulder mobility.
procedure: Preacher position (optionally with a stick); bending backward over a foam roller (with or without weight); rotations on the wall; rotations on the elbows; rotation in side-lying. Optional: windmill for the cervicothoracic junction (CTO).
notes: Background given by the page: sitting more than 7 h/day with less than 150 min/week of activity reduces thoracic mobility (Heneghan et al. 2018); increased kyphosis correlates with forward head posture, but posture is not uniformly associated with neck pain and disability (Joshi et al. 2019); upright posture improves affect and fatigue in people with depressive symptoms (Wilkes et al. 2017); increased kyphosis limits overhead mobility (Barrett et al. 2016). Pair with the thoracic strengthening page. Cho et al. 2017 is listed in the references but not discussed in the text.

title: Thoracic Spine Strengthening
purpose: Treatment: five exercises to strengthen the thoracic spine extensors and scapular muscles, the companion of the mobility page for changing posture.
structure: Thoracic extensors and scapular retractors/upward rotators; overhead position under load.
procedure: Squat with a kettlebell held overhead; front squats and overhead squats; wall or floor angels; Y-lifts (on a ball or standing); prone lying lifts with a stick.
notes: Same background paragraph as the thoracic mobility page (Heneghan 2018, Joshi 2019, Wilkes 2017, Barrett 2016). ⚠ The page's lead-in sentence says 'our 5 favorite exercises to mobilize the thoracic spine' although the list is strengthening exercises; the sentence was copied from the mobility page. Pair with the thoracic mobility page.
